summary: The root صرصر (SrSr) primarily describes a strong, loud, and piercing sound, often associated with wind. It conveys the idea of a violent, shrieking noise, like a whirlwind or a powerful gust.

provenance.lane: Edward William Lane, An Arabic-English Lexicon (1863-93), public domain. Digital text via Perseus, Tufts University, CC BY-SA 3.0 US.
provenance.summary: Editorial summary derived from the Lane entry. NOT Lane's own wording. Shown as a gloss only; the Lane text below is the source.

headword_note: Lane indexes geminate roots with two letters where the Corpus uses three; both spellings are resolved here. Kitab al-Ayn does the same, and also files some weak roots under a different third radical; those are resolved against the Corpus spelling and the al-Ayn headword is kept in the entry.
parts_note: parts[].k: d=Lane's English rendering, a=Arabic, p=apparatus/citation

entries.text: صر الجندب صريرا، وصرصر الأخطب صرصرة. وصر الباب يمصر، وكل صوت شبه ذلك فهو صرير إذا امتد، فاذا كان فيه تخفيف وترجيع في إعادة ضوعف كقولك: صرصر الأخطب صرصرة. وريح صرصر: ذات صر، ويقال: ذات صوت، والصرصر نعت لها من البرد.
قال الليث: صر الجندب يصر صريرا. وصر الباب يصر؛ وكل صوت شبه ذلك فهو صرير: إذا امتد، فإذا كان فيه تخفيف وترجيع في إعادة ضوعف.
الصَّرْصَرُ : صَرَّارُ الليل أو الصُّرْصُور.- من الرّياح: الشَّديدةُ ببردِها وصوتها وَأَمَّا عَادٌ فَأُهْلِكُوا بِرِيحٍ صَرْصَرٍ عَاتِيَة.
الصِّرُّ : شدّة البرد؛ ريحٌ صِرٌّ أي شديدة البرد/ والريحُ يا واقدُ ريحٌ صِرٌّ، كَمَثَلِ رِيحٍ فِيهَا صِرٌّ أَصَابَتْ حَرْثَ قَوْمٍ ظَلَمُوا أَنْفُسَهُمْ.-: شدة الصوت؛ أزعجه صِرُّ الأبواق النحاسية.

classical_note: Arabic-only entries from public-domain classical lexica, ordered by compiler death date. Tier 'root-semantic' (Maqayis) derives all senses of a root from one core idea. Tier 'interpretive' (Mufradat) cites hadith and takes theological positions and is not equivalent evidence. Tier 'earliest-disputed' (Kitab al-Ayn) marks a text whose attribution to al-Khalil ibn Ahmad (d. 786) is contested: the work records that his student al-Layth ibn al-Muzaffar completed it after his death, so the 786 date orders the entry but does not assert sole authorship. Tahdhib al-Lugha (al-Azhari, d. 980) is the earliest critical assessment of that text; al-Azhari himself calls it 'kitab al-Ayn attributed to al-Khalil'. Some Tahdhib entries are group-level: al-Azhari treats a set of root permutations together, and where a root has no entry of its own the headword shows the full permutation set.
